The difference now is that we assume the elements stored in the SSet are \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}-bit integers. It is not too hard to think of plenty of applications where the data---or at least the key that we use for sorting the data---is an integer. We will discuss three data structures, each building on the ideas of the previous. The first structure, the BinaryTrie performs all three SSet operations in $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}})$ time. content: \seclabel{binarytrie} \index{BinaryTrie@BinaryTrie} A BinaryTrie encodes a set of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}} bit integers in a binary tree. All leaves in the tree have depth \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}} and each integer is encoded as a root-to-leaf path. The path for the integer \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} turns left at level \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} if the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}th most significant bit of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} is a 0 and turns right if it is a 1. \figref{binarytrie-ex} shows an example for the case $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}=4$, in which the trie stores the integers 3(0011), 9(1001), 12(1100), and 13(1101).

content: The integers stored in a binary trie are encoded as root-to-leaf paths.

Because the search path \index{search path!in a BinaryTrie} for a value \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} depends on the bits of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, it will be helpful to name the children of a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{child}}[0]}} (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{left}}}}) and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{child}}[1]}} (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{right}}}}). These child pointers will actually serve double-duty. Since the leaves in a binary trie have no children, the pointers are used to string the leaves together into a doubly-linked list. For a leaf in the binary trie \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{child}}[0]}} (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{prev}}}}) is the node that comes before \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} in the list and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{child}}[1]}} (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}}}) is the node that follows \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} in the list. A special node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{dummy}}}}, is used both before the first node and after the last node in the list (see \secref{dllist}).

The \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation in a BinaryTrie is fairly straightforward. We try to follow the search path for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} in the trie. If we reach a leaf, then we have found \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}. If we reach a node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} where we cannot proceed (because \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is missing a child), then we follow \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{jump}}}}, which takes us either to the smallest leaf larger than \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} or the largest leaf smaller than \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}. Which of these two cases occurs depends on whether \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is missing its left or right child, respectively. In the former case (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is missing its left child), we have found the node we want. In the latter case (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is missing its right child), we can use the linked list to reach the node we want. Each of these cases is illustrated in \figref{binarytrie-find}.

content: \seclabel{xfast} \index{XFastTrie@XFastTrie} The performance of the BinaryTrie structure is not very impressive. The number of elements, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}, stored in the structure is at most $2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}$, so $\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\le \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}$. In other words, any of the comparison-based SSet structures described in other parts of this book are at least as efficient as a BinaryTrie, and are not restricted to only storing integers. Next we describe the XFastTrie, which is just a BinaryTrie with \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}+1}} hash tables---one for each level of the trie. These hash tables are used to speed up the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation to $O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}})$ time. Recall that the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation in a BinaryTrie is almost complete once we reach a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, where the search path for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} would like to proceed to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{right}}}} (or \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{left}}}}) but \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} has no right (respectively, left) child. At this point, the search uses \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{jump}}}} to jump to a leaf, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{v}}}}, of the BinaryTrie and either return \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{v}}}} or its successor in the linked list of leaves. An XFastTrie speeds up the search process by using binary search \index{binary search} on the levels of the trie to locate the node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. To use binary search, we need a way to determine if the node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} we are looking for is above a particular level, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, of if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is at or below level \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}. This information is given by the highest-order \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} bits in the binary representation of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}; these bits determine the search path that \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} takes from the root to level \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}. For an example, refer to \figref{xfast-path}; in this figure the last node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, on search path for 14 (whose binary representation is 1110) is the node labelled $11{\star\star}$ at level 2 because there is no node labelled $111{\star}$ at level 3. Thus, we can label each node at level \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} with an \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}-bit integer. Then, the node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} we are searching for would be at or below level \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} if and only if there is a node at level \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} whose label matches the highest-order \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} bits of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}.

The second \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation (on a treap) takes $O(\log r)$ time, where $r$ is the size of the treap. Later in this section, we will show that the expected size of the treap is $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}})$ so that this operation takes $O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}})$ time.\footnote{This is an application of \emph{Jensen's Inequality}: If $\E[r]=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}$, then $\E[\log r] \le \log w$.} Adding an element to a YFastTrie is also fairly simple---most of the time. The \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} method calls \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{xft}}.\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} to locate the treap, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}, into which \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} should be inserted. content: The first data structure to provide $O(\log\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}})$ time \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations was proposed by van~Emde~Boas and has since become known as the \emph{van~Emde~Boas} \index{van Emde Boas tree} (or \emph{stratified}) \index{stratified tree} \emph{tree} \cite{e77}. The original van~Emde~Boas structure had size $2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}$, making it impractical for large integers. The XFastTrie and YFastTrie data structures were discovered by Willard \cite{w83}. The XFastTrie structure is closely related to van~Emde~Boas trees; for instance, the hash tables in an XFastTrie replace arrays in a van~Emde~Boas tree. That is, instead of storing the hash table \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}}, a van~Emde~Boas tree stores an array of length $2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}}$.
